title: Cold winters did not clearly lower next-summer counts of Swedish resident birds relative to migrants in 1976-2025; partial migrants, mainly the wren, fell about 1.2% per 1 C colder winter
abstract: Question: does the North American result that warmer winters are followed by higher next-summer counts of resident birds relative to migrants (0.8-1.3% per C; four campaign studies) occur in Sweden? Data: Swedish Bird Survey (CC0) fixed routes 1997-2025 (6,024 same-observer year pairs, 597 routes), summer point routes 1976-2024 (9,287 pairs, 1,019 routes) and winter point routes 1975-2024; GHCN_CAMS monthly and E-OBS daily temperature. Method: species classes from the ratio of Christmas-count to summer prevalence in each region; change in log(1+count) of residents minus migrants on the same route and observer; December-February anomaly; route fixed effects; year-clustered intervals; placebo, permutation, bins, year fixed effects and winter-count tests. The plan was written before the fits. Results: the pre-registered resident-minus-migrant slope was +0.59% per C (95% CI -0.27 to 1.45) on fixed routes and +0.05% (-0.64 to 0.73) on point routes; pooled +0.25% (-0.28 to 0.79), below the North American estimates (z = -2.3 and -3.3). Winter counts showed no resident decrease after cold January-February. Partial migrants minus migrants gave +1.19% per C pooled (0.79 to 1.59; permutation p = 0.004 and 0.012; placebo near zero), but the wren (+9 to +10% per C) gave half of it; without the wren +0.6%. Among winter-present species, the most winter-present were the least sensitive. Daily cold days added nothing to the seasonal mean. In 15-year windows both contrasts were near zero or negative before 2000 and positive after about 2004 (post hoc). Limitations: count indices without detection models; with year fixed effects all slopes were uncertain, so year-level confounding is possible; no snow, ice or feeding data.

display.caption: Change in next-summer counts per +1 C December-February anomaly (95% CI) on Swedish fixed routes (circles) and summer point routes (squares). Residents minus migrants (pre-registered) is below the North American band (grey, sci:e2f6bd3d). Partial migrants minus migrants is positive; half of it goes away without the wren. Migrants alone and the next-winter placebo are near zero.

Species slopes relative to migrants against winter presence (Christmas-count / summer prevalence, log scale). The wren is the outlier. Fully resident, feeder-using species are near zero; the slope decreases with winter presence among winter-present species.

Slopes in 15-year windows of pair years. Both contrasts were near zero or negative in 1976-2000 point-route data and became positive after about 2004 in both surveys (post hoc pattern). Grey band: North American resident-minus-migrant estimate.

citations.reason: North American resident-minus-migrant winter slope (0.94% per C); Sweden whole-record slope is lower; same contrast design reused.
North American cold-winter result (1.33% per C); Sweden is lower; design reused.
North American resident, partial and migrant slopes and the cold-range amplification; Sweden does not show a larger resident effect at the cold range edge.
Daily cold nights added nothing to the DJF mean in North America; E-OBS cold days add nothing in Sweden either.
Earlier campaign use of the Swedish Bird Survey fixed routes.
Swedish birds gave no clear effect of warm previous seasons; this work tests winter instead.
Swedish birds did not repeat a North American range-position weather effect.
